checks.prompt: A team evaluates this tool for a product and concludes 'it sounds terrible, we should not use it'. They are building a neural text-to-speech service on top of an open model. What has the evaluation missed, and when would their conclusion actually be the right one?
checks.explanation: There are two products here and only one of them is what a modern stack uses. The high-value output is the phoneme string — produced from a per-language pronunciation dictionary plus letter-to-sound rules, with no audio synthesised at all — and it is what the open neural synthesisers are trained on and fed. The formant voice is the other half: tiny, deterministic, entirely offline, and unmistakably robotic, which makes it right for screen readers and embedded devices and wrong for a product voice.
options: They evaluated the wrong half. Its dominant role today is as the grapheme-to-phoneme front end: it converts text in a hundred-odd languages into phoneme strings using a pronunciation dictionary plus letter-to-sound rules, and nearly every open neural synthesiser — including whichever one they have chosen — consumes exactly those phonemes. Their conclusion is right only about the OTHER half, its formant voice, which is genuinely robotic and belongs in accessibility and embedded work rather than a product voice
They are right: the tool produces only audio, so a neural service must use a different front end entirely, and its phoneme output is an internal debugging aid
They are wrong because its voice is competitive with neural synthesis once the right voice data is installed; the phoneme output is a legacy feature
They are right for their case and wrong in general, because the tool's phonemes are proprietary to its own synthesiser and cannot be consumed by other models

checks.prompt: Explain this tool as a rules engine with two outputs. Describe the path text takes to become phonemes and what makes that path deterministic. Then explain the source-filter model its voice is built on, in enough detail to say why the engine is only a few megabytes and why it sounds the way it does. Finish by stating the sense in which it is a front end rather than a destination.
checks.expected: A correct answer must establish that nothing here is learnt or recorded. Text walks through a per-language pronunciation dictionary, with letter-to-sound rules handling words the dictionary does not contain, producing a phoneme string in a chosen notation — with stress marks riding along. Because it is a dictionary plus rules rather than a model or a recording, the same text with the same voice and flags gives byte-identical output every time. The source-filter model must be described concretely: a voiced sound starts as a buzzy glottal source — a pulse train at the pitch, or noise for fricatives — which is pushed through a handful of resonators tuned to the formant frequencies of the target sound, shaping the buzz into a recognisable vowel. The two consequences must be drawn: the engine is tiny because it stores rules and a few filter parameters rather than audio or weights, and it sounds robotic because there is no real vocal tract, only a few tuned band-pass filters, so the result is intelligible but obviously synthetic. The front-end point must be stated: in a modern stack you almost never ship this voice, you ship its PHONEMES into a better synthesiser, so knowing this tool means knowing the layer the whole open synthesis stack stands on. Noting that the phoneme-only mode produces phonemes without synthesising any audio, and that this is exactly what the standard Python bridge invokes, is a plus.

checks.prompt: A model trained on this tool's phonemes suddenly mispronounces everything after a deployment. Nothing about the model changed; the inference service was rebuilt from a newer base image and the phonemisation call was rewritten to use the Python bridge's defaults. What is the most likely explanation?
checks.explanation: This is the classic and expensive mismatch: a model is trained on a particular phoneme alphabet, and inference must produce that same alphabet. The Python bridge silently drops stress marks unless you ask for them and drops punctuation unless you preserve it — both of which the model may have been trained with and which cue prosody. An engine version change can shift symbols as well. The discipline is to pin the engine, the version, the language and the flags, and to use the same call on both sides.
options: The phoneme symbol set at inference no longer matches the one the model was trained on. Two things in this change can do it: the Python bridge drops stress marks by default unless asked to keep them, and punctuation is likewise dropped unless preserved — so a model trained with those symbols now receives a different alphabet. A different engine version can shift the symbols too. The rule is that training and inference must phonemise identically: same engine, same version, same language, same flags
A newer engine version improves pronunciation, so the model is receiving better phonemes than it was trained on and needs retraining to benefit; there is no way to keep the old behaviour
The Python bridge uses a different phoneme notation from the command-line tool, so the fix is to shell out to the command line instead, which always produces the notation models are trained on
The problem is the sample rate of the model rather than the phonemes, since the bridge normalises text to a different rate than the engine does

checks.prompt: Implement both halves. First the phoneme stream. Define `PRIMARY` and `SECONDARY` as the primary and secondary stress marks (U+02C8 and U+02CC) and `PUNCTUATION` as `".,;:!?"`. Write `strip_language_switches(stream)` returning the pair (stream with every parenthesised two-or-three-letter language marker removed and whitespace collapsed, list of the codes found in order). Write `parse_phonemes(stream, with_stress=True, preserve_punctuation=True)` returning a list of dicts with keys `phonemes`, `stress` and `trailing`: remove language markers first, split on whitespace, peel any trailing punctuation off each word, record `"primary"` if it contains the primary mark else `"secondary"` if it contains the secondary one else None, drop tokens with no phonemes left, and — when `with_stress` is false — strip the marks from `phonemes` and report the stress as None; when `preserve_punctuation` is false report `trailing` as the empty string. Write `phoneme_vocabulary(streams, with_stress=True)` returning the sorted set of individual characters across every token's `phonemes`, parsed with punctuation not preserved. Now the voice. Write `pulse_train(f0, sample_rate, n)` returning a list of `n` floats that is 1.0 at every multiple of `int(sample_rate / f0)` and 0.0 elsewhere. Write `resonator(source, freq, sample_rate, bandwidth=90.0)` applying the two-pole recurrence `y[n] = x[n] + a1*y[n-1] + a2*y[n-2]` with `r = exp(-pi * bandwidth / sample_rate)`, `a1 = 2*r*cos(2*pi*freq/sample_rate)` and `a2 = -(r*r)`, treating samples before the start as zero, and returning the list of outputs. Standard library only.
checks.explanation: The two option flags are the whole reason this parsing is worth writing out: turning stress off or punctuation off changes what a downstream model receives, silently, and the vocabulary assertions make the consequence explicit — the symbol set is two characters smaller, so a model trained on one alphabet is being fed another. That is the mismatch that makes a working model start mispronouncing everything after a rebuild. The language-switch markers are the same hazard in a different form: mixed-language input injects tokens that are not phonemes at all, and left in they pollute every symbol set derived from the corpus. The second half makes the voice concrete. Strike a resonator once and it rings at its own frequency and decays — that is all a formant is — and a narrower bandwidth rings longer, which is what a sharper resonance means. Sum three of them over one buzzy source and you have a vowel, built from a handful of numbers rather than a recording or a set of weights, which is exactly why the engine is a few megabytes and exactly why it sounds synthetic.
checks.test:
import math

STREAM = "hɛlˈoʊ wˈɜːld. ɪt kˈɒsts fˈaɪv dˈɒlɚz"

tokens = parse_phonemes(STREAM)
assert [t["phonemes"] for t in tokens] == \
    ["hɛlˈoʊ", "wˈɜːld", "ɪt", "kˈɒsts", "fˈaɪv", "dˈɒlɚz"], tokens
assert [t["stress"] for t in tokens] == \
    ["primary", "primary", None, "primary", "primary", "primary"], tokens
assert [t["trailing"] for t in tokens] == ["", ".", "", "", "", ""], tokens

# The two options that silently change what a downstream model receives.
bare = parse_phonemes(STREAM, with_stress=False)
assert [t["phonemes"] for t in bare] == \
    ["hɛloʊ", "wɜːld", "ɪt", "kɒsts", "faɪv", "dɒlɚz"], bare
assert all(t["stress"] is None for t in bare), bare
unpunctuated = parse_phonemes(STREAM, preserve_punctuation=False)
assert all(t["trailing"] == "" for t in unpunctuated), unpunctuated
assert parse_phonemes("ˌɪntənæʃənəl")[0]["stress"] == "secondary"
# A word carrying both marks is reported by its primary one.
assert parse_phonemes("ˌɪntəˈnæʃənəl")[0]["stress"] == "primary"

# Mixed-language text injects switch markers that would otherwise pollute the
# symbol set of every model trained on the stream.
mixed = "ðə (fr)bɔ̃ʒuʁ(en) wˈɜːld"
cleaned, switches = strip_language_switches(mixed)
assert switches == ["fr", "en"], switches
assert "(" not in cleaned and ")" not in cleaned, cleaned
assert cleaned.split() == ["ðə", "bɔ̃ʒuʁ", "wˈɜːld"], cleaned
assert [t["phonemes"] for t in parse_phonemes(mixed)] == \
    ["ðə", "bɔ̃ʒuʁ", "wˈɜːld"]
assert strip_language_switches("no markers here") == ("no markers here", [])

# THE mismatch that ruins a model: the symbol set depends on the options used, so
# phonemising at inference differently from training shifts the vocabulary.
corpus = [STREAM, "ˌɪntəˈnæʃənəl kˈoʊd"]
with_marks = phoneme_vocabulary(corpus, with_stress=True)
without = phoneme_vocabulary(corpus, with_stress=False)
assert "ˈ" in with_marks and "ˌ" in with_marks, with_marks
assert "ˈ" not in without and "ˌ" not in without, without
assert set(without) < set(with_marks), (without, with_marks)
assert len(with_marks) == len(without) + 2
assert "." not in with_marks, "punctuation is not a phoneme symbol"

# The source half of the voice: one impulse per pitch period, nothing between.
train = pulse_train(f0=100.0, sample_rate=1000, n=25)
assert train[0] == 1.0 and train[10] == 1.0 and train[20] == 1.0
assert sum(train) == 3.0, train
assert train[1:10] == [0.0] * 9, train
assert len(pulse_train(120.0, 22050, 2205)) == 2205
# One second of source holds about F0 impulses -- "about", because the period is a
# whole number of samples.
assert abs(sum(pulse_train(120.0, 22050, 22050)) - 120.0) <= 2.0

SR = 22050
N = 2205
impulse = [1.0] + [0.0] * (N - 1)


def crossings(signal):
    return sum(1 for i in range(1, len(signal))
               if (signal[i - 1] < 0) != (signal[i] < 0))


# The filter half: struck once, a resonator rings at ITS OWN frequency and decays.
# That is the whole trick -- a buzz shaped by a few tuned resonances.
low = resonator(impulse, 700, SR)
high = resonator(impulse, 2600, SR)
assert abs(crossings(low) - 2 * 700 * N / SR) < 0.1 * 2 * 700 * N / SR, crossings(low)
assert abs(crossings(high) - 2 * 2600 * N / SR) < 0.1 * 2 * 2600 * N / SR, crossings(high)
assert crossings(high) > crossings(low) * 3

early = max(abs(v) for v in low[:200])
late = max(abs(v) for v in low[-200:])
assert late < early, (early, late)
assert late < 0.5 * early, (early, late)

# A narrower bandwidth rings for longer -- the resonance is sharper.
sharp = resonator(impulse, 700, SR, bandwidth=30.0)
broad = resonator(impulse, 700, SR, bandwidth=300.0)
assert max(abs(v) for v in sharp[-200:]) > max(abs(v) for v in broad[-200:])

# Summing several resonators driven by the same source is the vowel: nothing about
# it is recorded or learnt, which is exactly why it is small and why it is robotic.
source = pulse_train(120.0, SR, N)
vowel = [0.0] * N
for frequency, bandwidth in [(700, 130), (1100, 90), (2600, 120)]:
    for index, value in enumerate(resonator(source, frequency, SR, bandwidth)):
        vowel[index] += value
assert len(vowel) == N
assert max(abs(v) for v in vowel) > 0.0
# Deterministic: the same inputs give byte-identical output every time.
assert vowel == [a + b + c for a, b, c in zip(
    resonator(source, 700, SR, 130), resonator(source, 1100, SR, 90),
    resonator(source, 2600, SR, 120))]

checks.prompt: A training pipeline is being set up on a mac. The Python bridge raises what looks like a crash rather than a missing-dependency message; once that is fixed, the phonemes for a script full of prices and abbreviations do not match what the team expected to see; and the resulting audio from a quick check is far too fast to follow. What are the three causes?
checks.explanation: Three separate practical traps. The Python bridge loads the shared library directly, so an installation into a non-standard prefix produces a crash-shaped failure rather than a helpful message, and an environment variable naming the library path is the fix. The engine normalises text before phonemising — expanding numbers, currency, dates and abbreviations into words, per language — so the phonemes reflect that expansion whether or not it is what you wanted; inspect them and normalise upstream if you need control. And the default speaking rate is genuinely fast, which matters most in accessibility use where a slower setting is clearer.
options: The bridge loads the shared library directly and can fail to find it when it was installed by a package manager into a non-standard prefix — an environment variable pointing at the library path fixes it, and the failure looks like a crash rather than a clear message. The unexpected phonemes are the engine's own text normalisation, which expands numbers, currency and abbreviations into words before phonemising, per language, whether or not you wanted it. And the default speaking rate is fast, around 175 words per minute, so a slower rate is worth setting for anything meant to be followed by ear
The crash means the engine is not installed at all; the phoneme differences mean the wrong language was selected; and the fast speech means the sample rate was misread as a rate parameter
All three come from using the older unmaintained binary rather than the maintained fork; installing the fork resolves the library lookup, the normalisation and the default rate together
The crash is a threading issue in the bridge; the phoneme differences mean stress marks were kept when they should have been dropped; and the fast speech is the pitch parameter, which is inverted

checks.prompt: Position this tool against a pure-Python alternative front end, a small neural offline synthesiser, and a cloud voice service. For each, say what it offers and what it costs relative to this one. Then advise two teams: one training a new open synthesis model on a multilingual corpus, and one shipping a screen reader for a low-power device with no network. Say what each should use and why, and name the one discipline the first team must follow.
checks.expected: A correct answer must position all three. A pure-Python alternative front end avoids the system dependency entirely, which is a genuine deployment simplification, at the cost of covering fewer languages and using a different symbol set — and the practical point is that this tool is what most open models have been trained against, so its symbol set is the de facto standard. A small neural offline synthesiser gives natural-ish real-time speech offline on modest hardware, and the relationship must be named: it USES this tool internally for its own text-to-phoneme step, so it is a destination rather than a competitor. A cloud voice service gives the highest naturalness and rich markup with no setup, at the cost of money, a network dependency, audio leaving the machine, and doing its own text-to-phoneme conversion. The recommendations must follow. The team training a multilingual model should use this tool as the front end: broad language coverage, deterministic output, and the symbol set the ecosystem is trained against. The screen-reader team should use its formant VOICE: a few megabytes, no network, no accelerator, deterministic, and intelligible — naturalness is not the requirement, and a slower speaking rate than the default is worth setting for clarity. The discipline the training team must follow is that phonemisation at inference must be identical to phonemisation at training: same engine, same version, same language and the same flags for stress and punctuation, because a different alphabet means a model that mispronounces everything. Noting that language-switch markers in mixed-language corpora must be handled rather than left in the symbol set is a plus.
